CHINA DESK: And so the Trump-Xi summit this week delivered what markets probably needed most.

That being no fresh escalation between the two largest economies in the world.

But beyond that, there wasn't much of any breakthrough either.

The clearest takeaway is the extension of the existing US-China trade truce by another two months to 10 January.

That keeps the existing tariffs regime in place and gives both sides more time to negotiate what Bessent has described as a potentially broader agreement.

So for now though, the difficult issues haven't really gone anywhere.

The US still wants China to step up agricultural purchases and to meet its commitments, while also raising concerns that China's rare earth deliveries have fallen short.

And honestly, that is hardly surprising given China's previous track record and how we saw the Phase One trade deal unfolded back in 2018-19.

From the inflation desk: A recession signal against a backdrop of strong data makes it a useful counterpoint for bond markets.

It gives Treasury bulls an argument just as 10-year yields sit above 5.2% and Fed hike odds are rising.

Markets are unlikely to react much for now, because Oxford itself plays down the signal and current data points the other way.

The warning matters more as a sign of what could go wrong if energy prices stay high and borrowing costs keep rising.

Any softening in spending data would give it far more weight quickly. --- Oxford Economics' US indicator says recession, but consumers and AI spending say otherwise.

It's a reminder that energy costs and a shrinking labour pool are building pressure beneath some very strong headline data.
